title: The five objections that stall a compliance business case
summary: Learn how to overcome five common objections that stall a compliance business case and build a stronger case for continuous compliance.
body_markdown:
If you manage vendor compliance or supply chain operations, you already know that deductions and rejections are expensive. The hard part isn’t believing it. The hard part is building a compliance business case for someone who controls the budget.


And most cases don’t fail on the numbers. They fail in the review room when five familiar objections surface and no one has answers ready. Here they are, with the answers.


## “We already have EDI.”


[Electronic data interchange](https://www.opentext.com/what-is/electronic-data-interchange) moves the document reliably. It does not judge the document against the trading partner’s current requirements.


A perfectly transmitted advance ship notice with a missing field is still a deduction. Transport and validation are different jobs, and doing the first one well has never guaranteed the second.


## “Our ERP already validates.”


It does, against your master data and your business rules. That’s worth having.


But the rules that actually generate penalties don’t live in your ERP. They live in a customer’s routing guide and a foreign tax authority’s schema, and they change on a schedule that has nothing to do with your release calendar. That’s a different problem from[ERP integration](https://www.opentext.com/what-is/erp-integration) , and it isn’t solved by the same work.


## “Our error rate is low.”


Low compared to what?


Ask for the exception rate rather than an impression.[Ardent Partners](https://ardentpartners.com/ap-metrics-that-matter-in-2025/) puts the average at roughly 14 percent of invoices requiring manual intervention, with best-in-class organizations at 9 percent. If nobody in the room can produce your number, that’s not a reassuring answer. That’s the finding.


## “We recover most of it anyway.”


Recovery works, and the money is real. But it happens at the most expensive end of the curve, and it never reaches everything.


More importantly, it does nothing to the rate at which errors occur. A better recovery function processes the same volume of failures more efficiently. Next year’s workload will be the same or larger. You’re paying skilled people to argue about mistakes you’ve already made.


## “We’ll deal with it when the mandate lands.”


Under a clearance model there is no soft landing. A non-compliant invoice isn’t a finding to remediate later. It’s a transaction that does not proceed.


That distinction is the one most likely to be misunderstood before a mandate goes live, and the one most expensive to learn afterward.[Five mistakes global companies make with e-Invoicing](https://blogs.opentext.com/five-mistakes-global-companies-make-with-e-invoicing/) covers the patterns that tend to surface late.


## What actually makes the case land


Having answers to those five gets you through the meeting. It doesn’t get you the budget. Three things do.


**Separate what you can prevent from what you can merely recover.** Sort your deductions into valid, invalid and unclear. Claim benefit only from the first group. If your organization already runs a recovery function, claiming the second is double counting, and someone in the review will spot it. Resisting that temptation is what makes the rest of your numbers credible.


**Lead with cash, not penalties.** Avoided penalties are the easiest number to produce and the least persuasive at executive level. Released working capital is harder to calculate and far harder to argue with. A disputed transaction is an open item that can’t be closed or forecast, and it ages in receivables looking like a late payment when it’s really an unresolved claim.


**Name your assumptions before someone finds them.** Don’t model 100 percent prevention. Rules change, partners onboard with requirements nobody has mapped, and some errors originate upstream of the network entirely. Use a conservative interception rate, show a sensitivity range, and let the case stand on the conservative end of it.


A reviewer who finds an assumption you already flagged will trust the rest of your model. A reviewer who finds one you hid won’t trust any of it.


## And one question to ask every vendor


Where exactly does validation happen, and can you show me a transaction being stopped before it transmits, rather than flagged after it lands?


That single question separates providers faster than any feature matrix will.
